# Recipes — chaining with the Project Discovery toolset

Design source: [`docs/spec.md#6-chaining-reference-implementations`](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#6-chaining-reference-implementations).
Recipes follow the cookbook grammar: *Problem* states the operational
need, *Solution* is the exact command to run, *Discussion* explains the
mechanics behind it. Every `Solution` was executed and its `Observation`
captured from the run; nothing here is aspirational. `pqscan` treats
upstream output as input lines and needs no flag unless a format requires
disambiguation.

``` {mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph DISC["Discovery layer — compose, not rebuild"]
    S[subfinder — domains]
    N[naabu — host:port truth]
    M[masscan / zmap — internet port sweep]
  end
  subgraph PQ["pqscan — cipher-configuration plane"]
    P1["fast — 1 handshake"]
    P2["deep — the offer-one matrix (≤24 standard, 80 full)"]
    P3["pq — PQ ladder + verdicts"]
  end
  subgraph SINK["Downstream"]
    J[jq triage / diffs]
    U[nuclei — tls tags]
    R[CSV / WAL / CI gate]
  end
  S --> P1
  N --> P1
  M --> P1
  P1 --> P2
  P1 --> P3
  P2 --> J
  P3 --> U
  P3 --> R
```

## Input chains

### Domain discovery → cipher truth

**Problem.** Enumerate the live subdomains of a zone and learn, per
endpoint, which key-exchange group and cipher suite the TLS stack
actually negotiates against a modern client — not what the
administrator configured, what the wire accepts.

**Solution.**

```bash
subfinder -d shain.io -silent \
  | httpx -silent -no-color \
  | pqscan -jsonl -o assets.jsonl
```

**Observation.** One schema-1 record per endpoint; this run's chain found
4 alive endpoints and the first record (the tools stamped at capture time:
subfinder v2.16.0 → httpx v1.12.0):

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"oi.shain.io","host":"oi.shain.io","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"sha256WithRSAEncryption","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"RSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** subfinder streams bare domains; httpx resolves and probes
them and answers `scheme://host` lines, which the spec grammar strips to
host specs natively — the chain needs no flag or adapter. The probe is
browser-grade: the ClientHello offers the
stdlib default group preference order (MLKEM hybrid first), offers ALPN
`h2,http/1.1`, and records what the server SELECTED — negotiation is
the assertion, no configuration parsing. Each upstream tool stays in
its lane; nothing in the chain re-implements another's job. When httpx
runs with `-csv`, its lines begin `url,status` and use the
`-from-httpx` flag (PQ-35); the text chain above requires nothing but
the tools.

### Port truth first

**Problem.** Only hosts that actually accept on a given port are worth
a probe handshake; probing closed sockets wastes the retry budget and
skews latency math.

**Solution.**

```bash
naabu -l domains.txt -p 443,8443,465,993 -silent \
  | pqscan -jsonl
```

**Observation.** naabu's `host:port` lines are first-class target
specs — one probe handshake, one record, per surviving socket (naabu 2.6.1
at capture time).

**Discussion.** naabu is the port-discovery plane: it answers with the
sockets that accept, which is exactly the input pqscan wants.
Certificates-directory collection and resumption analysis later reuse
the same records rather than re-dialing. `-from-naabu` additionally
covers naabu's bare-host-and-ports-block rendering; the `host:port`
form above is already first-class — and a saved render scans through
the flag form (the next recipe).

### PD dialect renders as files — -from-httpx / -from-naabu / -from-nuclei (PQ-35, PQ-55)

**Problem.** The Project Discovery tools render in their own dialects —
httpx speaks scheme-URI lines (`https://host:port`, an optional URL path
suffix), naabu speaks `host:port` (or a host line followed by its bare-port
block), and `nuclei -j` streams findings JSONL (one JSON finding per line,
its `matched-at` carrying the probed host). When the render is already on
disk the operator must not have
to clean it just to scan: the adapters accept the render the way any
target file is accepted.

**Solution.**

```bash
cat domains.txt | httpx -silent -ports 443,8443 -p 443,8443 -no-color > discovered.httpx   # the pinned capture (httpx v1.12.0)
pqscan -from-httpx discovered.httpx -jsonl

naabu -l domains.txt -p 443,8443,465,993 -silent > naabu.naabu   # the pinned capture (naabu 2.6.1)
pqscan -from-naabu naabu.naabu -jsonl

nuclei -l hosts.txt -silent -j > nuclei.jsonl   # the pinned capture (nuclei v3.11.1)
pqscan -from-nuclei nuclei.jsonl -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The imports executed with the real tools (each against its
pinned capture of that exact command); the renders upstream were verbatim, the records from the pqscan legs — the httpx
render's scheme/URI lines strip to host:port specs:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.org","host":"example.org","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":true,"state":"negotiated","negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":true,"h3_direct":true}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

and the naabu render's doubled `host:port` lines (`example.com:8443`,
`example.com:443` twice over — naabu renders per resolved address)
dedupe to one record per socket:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.com:8443","host":"example.com","ip":"","port":8443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

and the nuclei import: the pinned capture (nuclei v3.11.1, `hosts.txt =
scanme.sh`, the default template set) answers 28 findings on stdout; the
import walks the file and the one dedupe collapses them to the two
sockets the findings repeat — the ssh port's record (real error record:
the TCP plane reached an ssh service) and the https port's:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"scanme.sh:22","host":"scanme.sh","ip":"","port":22,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","suite":"","version":"","alpn_neg":""},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":0,"label":"","hndl":false,"summary":""},"error":"tls: first record does not look like a TLS handshake"}
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"scanme.sh:443","host":"scanme.sh","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":29,"group_name":"x25519","group_class":"classic","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":0,"label":"scan-error","hndl":false,"summary":"weak_classical_preferred(-5)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** The adapters feed the SAME composition -u/-l/-- use
(internal/target strips the dialect decoration; every line goes through
the one grammar), so one dedupe — host:port, first occurrence wins —
serves every input source in flag order; a bad line refuses the run
named by its flag (exit 64) rather than scanning a truncated list.
httpx's `-csv` (url,status) rows are a planned adapter
([PQ-61](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/issues/159)); the block
rendering of a naabu multi-port run (a host line followed by
bare-decimal port lines) parses through `-from-naabu` exactly as the
host:port lines do (the adapter's unit fixtures pin it). The
`-from-*` adapters walk files: the findings arrive on stdout of the
pinned `nuclei -j` capture, so the recipe redirects to the file the
import reads — a `-from-nuclei -` value is tried as a file name
(`open -: no such file or directory`, exit 64); `nuclei ... -j` writes
JSONL to stdout, `> findings.jsonl` puts it on disk.

### Internet scale — one box of a four-box pass

**Problem.** A /16-class estate must be swept for TLS posture without a
16-hour serial tail, and without one box's failure orphaning the run's
output.

**Solution.**

```bash
masscan -p 443 -iL cidrs.txt --rate=100000 --open-only -oX - \
  | pqscan -jsonl -o shard1.jsonl
```

**Observation.** masscan answers the port question at line rate;
pqscan answers the cipher-configuration question per surviving socket,
one schema-1 record stream out the other side.

**Discussion.** The two tools compose because their contracts are
narrow: masscan's `-oX -` and `--open-only` keep the pipe to what
accepts; pqscan adds the negotiated group, suite, ALPN, QUIC and
certificate blocks per host. Estate splitting is the flag's job now:
`-shard i/n` (PQ-24) filters the composed targets to one box's slice —
`fnv1a64(host:port) % n == i-1`, the shards disjoint and complete at a
fixed total — so the four boxes run the same list, each with its own
`-shard 1/4 … 4/4`, and the union of their records is the estate. The
stderr note carries the slice's count (`shard 1/4: N of M targets`);
each box bounds its own handshake budget with `-rate`/`-threads`
independently, and re-runs replay the WAL rather than re-dialing what
survived. Live partition proof on a 9-target list, both slice notes:

```text
pqscan: shard 1/2: 4 of 9 targets
pqscan: shard 2/2: 5 of 9 targets
```

### Target grammar and its refusals

**Problem.** The input contract must be exact: what pqscan accepts, and
precisely what it refuses — a scanner must fail closed on malformed
target specs, not mis-scan.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u example.com:8443 -jsonl      # host:port
pqscan -u 2001:db8::1 -jsonl           # v6 literal
echo http://example.org:8443 | pqscan -jsonl -   # scheme:// strips on the stdin alias
echo 'https://example.org:443/api' | pqscan -jsonl   # refused: a URL path suffix
printf '198.51.100.0/24\n' | pqscan -jsonl           # refused: CIDR spec
```

**Observation.** The first three run — the scheme strips off every spec
line (`-u`, `-l` lines, the piped stdin), leaving one schema-1 record
per target; `example.com:8443` negotiates and the unreachable v6
literal is a record with `error` set, never a refusal:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"example.com:8443","host":"example.com","ip":"","port":8443,"ptr":"","sni_used":""},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":false,"state":"skipped: no alt-svc h3 hint","negotiated":0,"group_name":"","group_class":"","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":false,"h3_direct":false}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

What refuses (exit 64, nothing scanned) — a URL path suffix on the
spec path (path stripping stays the adapters' business) and a CIDR
spec line (per-address expansion is planned):

```text
pqscan: URL path "/api" in target spec "https://example.org:443/api": a URL path is the -from-httpx adapter's decoration (-from-httpx FILE strips scheme and path; the spec path keeps host[:port])
```

```text
pqscan: -cidr target "198.51.100.0/24": cidr expansion is not supported
```

**Discussion.** The grammar takes bare hosts (443 default), `host:port`
forms, IPv4/IPv6 literals (bracketed v6 with port), `scheme://host[:port]`
(the scheme strips on every spec line), `i/n` shard specs, and the
stdin forms: the pipe is the implicit default input (no marker needed),
`-l -` is the explicit stdin-file alias, `--` composes beside `-u`/`-l`.
Every flag also parses under two dashes (`--mode` is `-mode`), and the
completions offer both spellings. Specs dedupe by host:port in input
order. Unreachable endpoints are NOT refusals —
they are records with `error` set, which the failure-taxonomy recipe
below classifies. CIDR spec lines refuse — per-address expansion is not
supported (the grammar parses the class; the expansion is the boundary).

## Modes: fast, deep, pq

### Deep standard — the bounded ≤24-probe profile

**Problem.** Beyond the one fast handshake: which named groups the
server refuses or accepts rung by rung, what the QUIC plane answers for
the same rungs, the ML-DSA signature ladder, and the HRR demand — the
structural ladders without paying the full matrix's cost on every asset.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The record gains a `deep` block; this run's counts and
a finding excerpt (the 22nd finding is the HRR row):

```text
mode=standard attempted=22 ok=2 rejected=8
group/4585    rejected   alert 40
group/4586    rejected   alert 40
group/4587    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4589    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4590    rejected   alert 40
group/25      rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/29      accepted   negotiated x25519, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
sigalg/mldsa65 refused    not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
hrr/x25519-shareless  accepted   hrr: the server requested group x25519 (29)
```

with the text line carrying the counts tail `deep=standard:22p/2ok/8rej`
(the remaining 12 of the 22 findings are the `refused` rows: three
classical groups the stdlib cannot offer, three QUIC rungs ditto, three
ML-DSA sigalgs, three resumption vectors — each row its own finding).

**Discussion.** The profile handshake runs first and its facts PRUNE
the plan (spec §7.4 phase 1): the negotiated group, the negotiated
(suite, version) pair, the negotiated version, the certificate probe
and the QUIC rung the profile already answered never re-probe. The
plan then cuts to the ≤24 budget through the documented prune classes —
adjacent suites first, then suites on the observed version, then all
remaining suites, then foreign-version probes, then the classic
signature algorithms — never touching the forced-group ladder, the
ML-DSA sigalgs, the cert probe, the 0-RTT and HRR probes. On a modern
host (the live reference above) that leaves exactly the structural
ladders: the group and QUIC rungs, the ML-DSA ladder, resumption, HRR
— the legacy suite and version hunt lives in `-deep full`. Per-kind
dispatch: a group probe offers ONE named group — a real share where
the toolchain has one, a share-less raw offer where it does not (the
obsolete-Kyber oracle). `refused` rows are locally not-offerable
probes: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list
and the resumption plane is not instrumented yet — the finding's
detail says exactly that, so a `refused` row is a capability boundary,
not a server answer. The HRR probe extracts the group the server
DEMANDED when the client withheld a share.

### Deep full — the complete offer-one matrix

**Problem.** Exhaustive coverage: every suite × version pair (the
secure default list AND the legacy/insecure suites), every registry
group, the signature-algorithm surface, resumption vectors, the QUIC
plane's rungs and the HRR hop — the complete offer-one matrix, each row
one handshake.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live) The record's `deep` block counts:

```json
{"mode":"full","attempted":80,"ok":28,"rejected":33}
```

(the remaining 19 findings are the `refused` rows). Sample suite
findings (the legacy hunt lives here):

```text
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.0   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.2
suite/TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256@1.3           refused    not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2     rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
```

**Discussion.** 80 probes, none pruned by observed facts: 4 versions,
11 registry groups (4585–4590 plus the classical set), 47 suite×version
pairs (the list auto-tracks `crypto/tls`, so a Go upgrade that gains a
suite grows the matrix), 7 signature algorithms (incl. the ML-DSA
codepoints), 1 certificate, 3 resumption vectors, 1 HRR, and the 6
QUIC-plane rungs. Standard never exceeds its 24-probe budget; `full`
trades the budget for coverage and is the run you point at ONE asset
you care about, not an estate.

### -mode pq — the forced PQ ladder

**Problem.** Which post-quantum groups will this server accept when
forced rung by rung — independent of the client's default preference
order — and does it still negotiate an obsolete draft.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode pq -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live) The record's handshake block carries the
ladder's first ACCEPTED hybrid; the ladder lands as a deep-mode-shaped
block — `mode:"pq"` with the counts `8 attempted / 1 ok / 7 rejected`
and one finding per rung — and the `-text` line rides the same counts
as the tail `deep=pq:8p/1ok/7rej`:

```text
group/4588   accepted    negotiated X25519MLKEM768, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
group/4590   rejected    alert 40
group/25497  rejected    alert 40
group/25498  rejected    alert 40
```

under `-explain` the ladder's reading names the accepted rung and the
refusals in operator words:

```text
  - deep: the forced PQ ladder made 8 offers: 1 accepted, 7 refused with the server's reasons, 0 not-offerable; accepted: group/4588; each forced PQ-only group came back refused unless the server truly speaks it — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

**Discussion.** `-mode pq` runs the forced ladder 4585–4590 plus the
Kyber drafts (25497/25498). The verdict rides the record's `pq` block:
a draft-HRR
acceptance trips `pq.hndl` — the harvest-now-decrypt-later flag —
because material intercepted against a draft-group handshake decrypts
when the draft is broken, regardless of how modern the rest of the
suite looks. The obsolete-Kyber oracle (the share-less offer of 25497,
answered by the HRR demanding the draft) is the finding that seeds the
compat-ladder decisions. This mode is the one to schedule FIRST on any
asset whose `pq.label` reads below `pq-ready-hybrid`.

## The cipher questions

### Which ciphers does the server accept?

**Problem.** For a given host: does it support — or refuse — a
specific cipher suite. Is ChaCha20-Poly1305 in its modern set? Is the
legacy CBC family still open on TLS 1.0–1.2? Answer from the wire,
one handshake per question.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("suite/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live, excerpt)

```text
suite/TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256@1.3            refused   not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256@1.3      refused   not-offerable on tls-1.3: crypto/tls offers the fixed 1.3 suite set (offer-one is not client-restrictable)
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.0   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
suite/TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA@1.2   accepted   negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.2
```

**Discussion.** Each suite probe is its OWN handshake offering ONE
suite (offer-one / observe-accept — never a shared negotiation, so an
`accepted` row is unambiguous). TLS 1.0–1.2 suites are individually
forceable; TLS 1.3's ciphers ride one fixed set that
`crypto/tls` cannot restrict, so those rows read `refused` with the
reason in the detail — and the 1.3 SET acceptance is still visible in
the record's `handshake.suite`, set by the profile handshake. To ask
about a suite NOT in the registry list, the `-probe-suite` override
(planned) offers arbitrary suites; until it lands the matrix covers
the stdlib lists auto-tracked per Go release.

### Which TLS versions does the server still accept?

**Problem.** The legacy-version floor is the classic audit question:
is TLS 1.0/1.1 still on? Which legacy stacks still serve?

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -deep full -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("version/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result): \(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
version/1.0    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.0
version/1.1    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA, tls-1.1
version/1.2    accepted: negotiated TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.2
version/1.3    accepted: negotiated TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
```

**Discussion.** The version hunt runs in the `full` matrix: the standard
plan's documented prune classes drop the foreign-version probes once the
budget gets tight (the live reference's standard run planned none — its
structural ladders already filled the 24-probe budget). Pair it with the
suite rows: the 1.0/1.1 answers above negotiated an ECDSA-keyed CBC
suite — a legacy-only answer the fast
plane would never surface, because the browser-grade handshake always
lands 1.3. THIS is why the deep modes exist: the fast record says
"modern and hybrid", the deep findings say "and still answering on a
decade-old CBC stack".

### Which PQ groups does the server accept when probed?

**Problem.** Not negotiation-by-default — forced acceptability: which
of the ML-KEM hybrids (4585–4590) and legacy drafts does this server
take, and with what alert when it refuses.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("group/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
group/4585    rejected   alert 40
group/4586    rejected   alert 40
group/4587    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4589    rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/4590    rejected   alert 40
group/25      rejected   remote error: tls: handshake failure
group/26      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/27      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/28      refused    not-offerable locally: tls: no supported key exchange methods (CurveIDs)
group/29      accepted   negotiated x25519, suite TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, tls-1.3
```

**Discussion.** `rejected` rows carry the server's own alert: alert 40
is the group refused at the ClientHello; the `tls: handshake failure`
form is the server's stricter mid-handshake shaping — either way the
answer is "the server answered and said no", a RESULT, not a failure.
`refused` rows are the honest capability boundary (no stdlib share
exists for that codepoint yet). The HRR finding closes the set: when
the client withholds everything, what the server DEMANDS in its
HelloRetryRequest is the last acceptability datum.

### Which signature algorithms are offered / possible?

**Problem.** PQ certificate signatures (ML-DSA/SLH-DSA) on the wire:
what can be proven today, and where the boundary is.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -jsonl \
  | jq -r '.deep.findings[] | select(.probe | startswith("sigalg/")) | "\(.probe)\t\(.result)\t\(.detail)"'
```

**Observation.** (live; every sigalg row refuses with its reason)

```text
sigalg/mldsa44   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
sigalg/mldsa65   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
sigalg/mldsa87   refused   not-offerable: the raw ClientHello path pins its signature_algorithms list (custom-list offers are not offered)
```

**Discussion.** What IS provable today: the certificate analytics in
the record's `cert` block — the leaf chain's signature algorithm
(`ecdsa-with-SHA256`), key algorithm, PQ-ness, and the dual-cert rule
(`cert.dual` = true when a classical-signed and a PQ-signed member
coexist in the offered chain). Custom signature_algorithms offers in
the raw ClientHello are the planned surface; until then the sigalg
probe rows state the boundary per finding rather than vanishing. The
`-probe-sigalgs` override (planned) will offer arbitrary lists.

## Debugging and fault logging

### Logging a fault: -debug and the live stream

**Problem.** When a run misbehaves — or reports a scan — the operator
needs the full decision trail, human-readable, live.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u 127.0.0.1:64444 -debug
```

**Observation.** (live, stderr + the record on stdout)

```text
  21:43:45.775 [info][config] run : diagnostics armed  positional_args= version=0.0.1
  21:43:45.775 [info][engine] pipeline : multi-target scan started  max_window=1 progress_every=50 rate=0 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [error][tls] scan 127.0.0.1: TCP probe refused (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused)
  21:43:45.776 [info][engine] pipeline 127.0.0.1:64444: progress reported  done=1 total=1
pqscan: progress: 1/1 targets scanned
127.0.0.1:64444 group=- class=- suite=- version=- cert=-/- error=dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused
  21:43:45.776 [info][output] emit 127.0.0.1: record emitted  format=text
── pqscan diagnostics ── schema 1 ── 0.0.1 (go1.27.2, darwin/arm64)
run: 2026-10-20T21:43:45.775767+11:00 → 2026-10-20T21:43:45.776132+11:00
flags: debug=true u=127.0.0.1:64444
events (5):
  21:43:45.775 [info][config] run : diagnostics armed  positional_args= version=0.0.1
  21:43:45.775 [info][engine] pipeline : multi-target scan started  max_window=1 progress_every=50 rate=0 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [error][tls] scan 127.0.0.1: TCP probe refused (dial tcp 127.0.0.1:64444: connect: connection refused)
  21:43:45.776 [info][engine] pipeline 127.0.0.1:64444: progress reported  done=1 total=1
  21:43:45.776 [info][output] emit 127.0.0.1: record emitted  format=text
summary: 5 events (1 errors, 0 warnings)
```

**Discussion.** Every decision point emits: ladder steps, QUIC
handshakes, refusal classifications, timeouts, rate/breaker decisions,
WAL writes, emissions. The `[level][domain]` prefix is the taxonomy —
`[error][tls]` vs `[warn][quic]` vs `[info][engine]` — and the trailer
block restates the run's shape (flags, window, totals) so a pasted
stderr is self-describing.

### Attaching the machine-readable fault: -debug-out

**Problem.** A ticket needs the structured event log, not a paste; the
downstream tooling wants to query by domain, level and target.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u hostile.internal -quic-off -debug -debug-out diag.json
jq -c '.summary' diag.json
jq -r '.events[] | "\(.level)[\(.domain)] \(.op) \(.target // "-")"' diag.json
```

**Observation.** (live)

```json
{"events":5,"errors":1,"warnings":0}
```

```text
info[config] run -
info[engine] pipeline -
error[tls] scan hostile.internal
info[engine] pipeline hostile.internal
info[output] emit hostile.internal
```

**Discussion.** `-debug-out` writes the full event log as JSONL beside
the run (independent of `-debug`'s stderr stream — arm either or
both). The event objects carry level, domain, op, target, error and
timing — the same stream the live view renders. BUG REPORTS AND
SCAN-TOUCHING FEATURE REQUESTS attach `-debug -debug-out diag.json`
output: the issue templates demand it, because the event log is the
only reproduction that shows the tool's decisions.

### The failure taxonomy: reading scan results correctly

**Problem.** A red error line is not always a failure — a refused
OFFER is a finding, a timeout is an estate problem, a breaker is the
tool protecting itself. Triage needs the classes.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl \
  | jq -r 'select(.error != "") | "\(.target.host): \(.error)"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

**Observation.** The classes and their meanings:

| class | reads as | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| refused (dial) | `connect: connection refused`, `no route to host` | nothing listening; the target is wrong or down |
| timeout / deadline | `i/o timeout`, `context deadline exceeded` | the deadline ladder (connect 2 s / handshake 4 s / probe 8 s, ±20 % jitter) fired — throttled or silently dropping |
| rejected (server) | `alert 40`, `tls: handshake failure`, `tls: bad certificate` | the server ANSWERED and said no — a finding, not a fault |
| refused (local) | `not-offerable locally: …` | pqscan cannot construct the offer — a tool capability boundary, stated in the record |
| breaker open | `breaker open` | the host's own failure budget tripped; no dial attempted for subsequent targets |

**Discussion.** Only the first two classes mean "the estate is
unreachable"; `rejected` rows are ANSWERS (they feed the deep modes'
findings and the rubric); the local `refused` class should be zero for
every supported codepoint and is regression-tested per release. The
breaker row is the congestion plane doing its job — see the hostile-
hosts recipe. The exit code stays zero for completed scans regardless
of per-target error records; a non-zero exit means the RUN itself
failed (binary fault, WAL unwritable, flag misuse).

### Hostile or flaky targets: rate, window, breakers

**Problem.** An estate with dead subnets must not drag the run, nor
pound a struggling host into further misery.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -rate 2000 -threads 64 -jsonl
```

**Observation.** (live, `-rate 5` on 3 closed local ports — `time`
shows the bucket's launch-cadence floor; the same run uncapped for
contrast)

```text
real    0m0.412s        pqscan -l t3.txt -rate 5   (3 launches ≥ 0.4s at 5 rps: the bucket's floor)
real    0m0.019s        pqscan -l t3.txt           (uncapped)
```

**Discussion.** `-rate` meters launches through a token bucket;
`-threads` sets the in-flight cap and AIMD owns the window: grow on
successes, halve on probe timeouts, floor at one. A host failing
consecutively trips ITS breaker: later targets on that host emit
`breaker open` error records WITHOUT a dial (the taxonomy table's
row). After the cooldown the breaker half-opens on a single probe and
closes on success. The defaults are unbounded-sequential; the flags
make the run estate-shaped.

### Crash-resume and the WAL journal

**Problem.** A long estate run dies at 80 %. Do not pay for 80 % of
the handshakes twice, and do not lose the completed set.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -o out.jsonl          # interrupted mid-run
pqscan -l estate.txt -o out.jsonl -resume  # scans only the remainder
```

**Observation.** (live)

```text
pqscan: resume: WAL out.wal: 1 of 3 targets already complete; scanning 2
pqscan: progress: 2/2 targets scanned
```

**Discussion.** The WAL is an append-only journal beside the output
file: every completed target lands fsync-batched under a monotone
sequence and a run id. A SIGKILL loses nothing but the socket in
flight — the output may be short, the journal is not. A resume
replays completed targets into the output (records ride through
unchanged) and probes only the difference; a run restarted with a
different target list composes: the journal's keys are `host:port`,
deduped in input order. The SLO: CI measures a 50-target farm at ≤ 6 s
wall for the half.

## Records, output and triage

### The record and its consumers

**Problem.** A scan's value is downstream readability: triage, diffs,
and machine consumption without a bespoke parser each time.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl -o estate.jsonl        # streaming records
pqscan -l estate.txt -csv  -o estate.csv           # spreadsheet-shaped
pqscan -l estate.txt -urls | nuclei -silent -tags tls   # URL re-emission
```

**Observation.** The CSV contract is the record's flat form — 25
columns, header on the first line:

```text
target,host,port,ptr,sni,negotiated,group_name,group_class,suite,version,alpn,quic_state,quic_group,udp_blocked,cert_sig_alg,cert_sig_pq,cert_key_alg,cert_key_pq,cert_dual,pq_score,pq_label,pq_hndl,pq_summary,error,ts
google.com,google.com,443,,,4588,X25519MLKEM768,pq_hybrid,TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,tls-1.3,h2,negotiated,X25519MLKEM768,false,ecdsa-with-SHA256,false,ECDSA,false,false,40,pq-partial,false,negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40),,2026-10-20T10:25:32.034802Z
```

**Discussion.** The writers are hand-rolled — no reflection, no
`encoding/json` on the hot path — so the column order in the CSV and
the key order in the JSONL are pinned by goldens in the test tree; a
contract change is a visible golden diff in review, never a silent
serde behavior change. Default output is the text one-liner for eyes;
`-jsonl` is the machine form; `-csv` the archival form; `-urls` the
re-emission for URL-taking scanners.

### The PQ verdict view

**Problem.** An estate's post-quantum readiness must be a one-line
triage: where is the migration stuck, and what must move first.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l estate.txt -jsonl \
  | jq -c '{target:.target.host, group:.handshake.group_name, class:.handshake.group_class, score:.pq.score, label:.pq.label, hndl:.pq.hndl}'
```

**Observation.** One compact object per target (live; `-o` sends the
records to the file instead of the pipe, so the triage jq reads stdout
directly):

```json
{"target":"google.com","group":"X25519MLKEM768","class":"pq_hybrid","score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false}
{"target":"example.org","group":"X25519MLKEM768","class":"pq_hybrid","score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false}
```

**Discussion.** The record scores itself: `pq.score` is the weighted
rubric sum, `pq.label` its band (`pq-ready` ≥ 80, `pq-ready-hybrid` ≥
60, `pq-partial` ≥ 40, `pq-missing` ≥ 1), and `pq.hndl` the
harvest-now-decrypt-later flag — true whenever an obsolete draft group
accepted the handshake, because material intercepted against such
handshakes decrypts when the draft breaks. Escalate on `hndl`;
treat the sub-60 bands as the worklist. The rubric feeds on the
negotiated-plane facts today; the certificate signature analytics ride
the `cert` block, and `pq.score` rises through the same field as the
deep findings wire in.

### The verdict in words: -explain

**Problem.** The text line's key=value fields are dense; a ticket or a
handoff needs the record read in sentences — what the verdict means,
which layer is the gap, and (when nothing negotiated) what the error
class suggests.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u google.com -explain
```

**Observation.** (live) Under each text line, one reading block:

```text
google.com:443 group=X25519MLKEM768 class=pq_hybrid suite=TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 version=tls-1.3 alpn=h2 quic_neg=X25519MLKEM768 quic_class=pq_hybrid cert=ecdsa-with-SHA256/ECDSA pq=pq-partial(40)
  - verdict: pq-partial 40/100. The negotiated key exchange is post-quantum; the certificate layer is classical — see the lines below.
  - key exchange: X25519MLKEM768 (pq_hybrid) — post-quantum hybrid: ML-KEM-768 + X25519. Session traffic is protected from later decryption by a quantum computer; the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk does not apply while this group negotiates.
  - certificate: classical identity (ECDSA key, ecdsa-with-SHA256 signature). Rotating to a PQ-signed (or dual) certificate at the next renewal closes the readiness gap.
  - quic: X25519MLKEM768 (pq_hybrid) on the UDP plane — the same post-quantum verdict applies to h3 traffic.
```

Deep and pq runs get the plan reading. On `-mode deep` the executed plan
reads in operator words — the probe roll-up, the offered-one matrix and
the accepted rows (live, `pqscan -u google.com -mode deep -explain`):

```text
  - deep: the executed standard plan ran 22 probes: 2 accepted, 8 refused with the server's reasons, 12 not-offerable; the offered-one matrix read: group ladder 1/10, quic rungs 0/5, sigalg ladder 0/3, resumption vectors 0/3, hrr probe 1/1; accepted: group/29; hrr/x25519-shareless — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

On `-mode pq` the ladder wording names the accepted rungs and treats the
refusal mass as the expected default:

```text
  - deep: the forced PQ ladder made 8 offers: 1 accepted, 7 refused with the server's reasons, 0 not-offerable; accepted: group/4588; each forced PQ-only group came back refused unless the server truly speaks it — the per-probe detail lives in the jsonl findings.
```

and a refused dial gets the error-class hint (the record's zero-populated
probe blocks read as their never-ran lines):

```text
  - quic: the lane never ran on this record.
  - error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:65000: connect: connection refused — no handshake was reached: the endpoint is unreachable on this port (closed or filtered); no cipher verdict is possible.
```

**Discussion.** `-explain` is a `-text`-only selector: the machine
formats refuse it (exit 64, `pqscan: -explain applies to text output
only (drop the -jsonl selector)`). Every tail the text line carries
(`cert=sig/key`, the `deep=` counts, `ptr=`/`sni=` enrichment) has its
counterpart in the reading — the human format tells the same story the
machine formats carry.

### Self-explanation: -version and the completion scripts

**Problem.** Support and scripting need the tool's own identity and
shell integration, generated — not hand-maintained flag lists.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -version
source <(pqscan -completion bash)     # zsh: pqscan -completion zsh > .../site-functions/_pqscan
```

**Observation.** (live) Source builds print the bare stamp; the
completion registers under the flag's name in bash:

```text
pqscan 0.0.1
```

```text
complete -F _pqscan_completions pqscan
```

**Discussion.** The scripts are generated from the same flag surface
the `-h` help renders — every implemented flag, the `-mode`/`-deep`
`-sni`/`-completion` value lists, file completion where a flag takes a
path, and BOTH dash spellings (`--word` parses anywhere `-word` does,
and the completions offer both). Install one-liners and the persisted
locations live in INSTALL.md; re-run the generator after upgrading so
the completion matches the binary. The `-version` stamp is the
release stamp on packaged builds.

## Downstream

### Feed nuclei

**Problem.** Hand payload-scanning to the scanner that does payloads;
keep the handshake facts where they belong.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -l assets.txt -urls | nuclei -silent -tags tls
```

**Observation.** `-urls` emits `scheme://host:port` per target — the
URL list any URL-taking scanner wants; the handshake/certificate/PQ
facts stay in pqscan's record stream (the `-o` file in the same run).

**Discussion.** The pipeline's stages compose by contract, not intent:
records stream in input order, WAL alongside, both consumed
independently. The reverse also holds: masscan/naabu's output feeds
IN, nuclei's output feeds OUT — pqscan never inspects payloads.

### The estate PQ calendar

**Problem.** Readiness is a trajectory, not a snapshot: leadership
wants the delta week over week, not a wall of JSON.

**Solution.**

```bash
# nightly, cron'd; the same target list, deterministic input order
pqscan -l estate.txt -csv -o /var/pqscan/$(date +%F).csv
diff /var/pqscan/yesterday.csv /var/pqscan/today.csv > /var/pqscan/pq-movement.diff
```

**Observation.** Repeat runs against a fixed list are comparable:
input order + first-occurrence dedupe make the stream deterministic;
the ts column orders the movement.

**Discussion.** Keep the diffs, not the runs: a day's movement is a
handful of rows — who moved up a band, who regressed, whose `hndl`
still fires. A CI job on the same contract gates merges in the
estate's own repos: a PR that demotes a band shows up as a failing
parity check.

### Reverse-DNS workflow — IP ranges in, domains out (PQ-26)

**Problem.** IP sweeps lose the SNI a domain run has; certificate
analytics without hostname context loses meaning on shared
infrastructure.

**Solution.**

```bash
pqscan -u 8.8.8.8:443 -ptr -sni auto -certs-dir certs/ -jsonl
```

**Observation.** The literal is resolved pre-probe and the record carries
the answer verbatim — the PTR-derived candidate is the SNI, the record's
`ptr` and `sni_used` both fill, and the PEM export leaves the leaf
behind for downstream tools:

```json
{"schema":1,"mode":"fast","target":{"input":"8.8.8.8:443","host":"8.8.8.8","ip":"","port":443,"ptr":"dns.google","sni_used":"dns.google"},"handshake":{"negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","suite":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","version":"tls-1.3","alpn_neg":"h2"},"quic":{"attempted":true,"state":"negotiated","negotiated":4588,"group_name":"X25519MLKEM768","group_class":"pq_hybrid","discovered":{"alt_svc_h3":true,"h3_direct":true}},"cert":{"sig_alg":"ecdsa-with-SHA256","sig_pq":false,"key_alg":"ECDSA","key_pq":false,"dual":false},"pq":{"score":40,"label":"pq-partial","hndl":false,"summary":"negotiated_pq_hybrid(+40)"},"error":""}
```

**Discussion.** `-ptr` builds the run's pool (bounded: 4 workers, a 2s
budget, a 1024-entry LRU of positives — misses never cache) off the
system resolver; `-sni` picks the candidate rule (`auto`/`ptr-then-ip`
prefer the PTR name and fall back to the literal; `ip-only` always the
literal; the record's `sni_used` carries the candidate actually used).
`-certs-dir` writes the scan's end-entity certificate per host
(`<dir>/<host>.pem`) so a scan feeds a CA/policy pass without a
re-dial. A literal whose PTR never resolves scans on the literal and
records the miss as an empty `ptr` — enrichment is never a blocker.
Bulk PTR enumeration at massive scale stays with massdns or zdns:
pre-filter there, hand the FQDNs forward.

## The flag map (live, landing, planned)

| Recipe topic | Flags / mode | State |
|---|---|---|
| one handshake, both planes | -u, -l and -l - (the stdin-file alias), the implicit piped stdin, -- (the bare marker), -jsonl or -json, -csv, -urls, -o, -resume, -quic-always, -quic-off, -debug, -debug-out | live |
| deep modes | -mode deep with -deep standard\|full | live |
| forced PQ ladder | -mode pq | live |
| the verdict in words | -explain (under -text; the machine formats refuse it) | live |
| self-explanation | -version, -completion bash\|zsh | live |
| rate/window/breakers | -rate, -threads | live |
| PD adapters | -from-httpx, -from-naabu, -from-nuclei (one pinned capture command each, version-stamped in the recipes) | live |
| sharding | -shard i/n | live |
| identity hooks | -ptr, -sni, -certs-dir | live |
| port selection | -p ([spec §5.1](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#51-targeting-and-discovery)) | planned |
| profile config | -config, PQSCAN_* env ([spec §8](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#8-cli-surface)) | planned |
| legacy module | -legacy heartbleed,ccs,robot ([spec §8](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#8-cli-surface)) | planned |
| probe overrides | -probe-suite, -probe-group, -probe-sigalgs, -probe-version ([spec §5.4](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#54-handshake-engine-capability-checklist-client-plane)) | planned |
| TLS fingerprints | -client-fingerprint, -jarm ([spec §5.4](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#54-handshake-engine-capability-checklist-client-plane)) | planned |
| sort/fields/silent/stats | -sorted, -fields, -silent, -stats ([spec §5.7](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#57-output-and-chainability)) | planned |
| dial budgets | -timeout, -connect-timeout, -retries ([spec §7.3](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#73-budgets-and-fairness-the-numbers-that-make-it-fast-and-safe)) | planned |
| scale ceilings | -c, -dns-threads ([spec §7.3](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#73-budgets-and-fairness-the-numbers-that-make-it-fast-and-safe)) | planned |
| the HTTP probe | -http ([spec §5.3](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/blob/main/docs/spec.md#53-protocol-coverage-matrix)) | planned |
| CIDR expansion | -cidr and CIDR spec lines (the [PQ-16](https://github.com/shsingh/pqscan/issues/39) deferral notice) | planned |

The usage-drift gate in CI keeps USAGE.md and this map honest: a flag
without a man-page row, or a row outside the implemented+planned set,
fails the PR. Every planned row names the spec row it earns under; the
flag map is where a new operator starts.
